storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the oath from the previous beat and turns it into the setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lodge as a physical room of secrecy.

image.subject: a candle-lit 18th-century library at night, a wooden table piled with books and a handwritten manifesto, no one in the room

storyboard.claim: The order's aim was to overthrow superstition and monarchy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manifesto on a desk in a library, showing the plan on paper.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the lodge oath to the goal the oath served.
storyboard.addedInformation: The plan was written down, not only whispered.

image.subject: an 18th-century Bavarian university lecture hall at dusk, rows of empty wooden benches under a tall window of pale light

storyboard.claim: The group called itself the Illuminati and drew on the Enlightenment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A university hall at dusk, the setting where the reason-based ideas were taught.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the plan to the intellectual source of the name.
storyboard.addedInformation: The Illuminati came out of university teaching.

image.subject: a late-18th-century Bavarian university professor in his late twenties, slim, powdered-hair style, dark frock coat with a white cravat, standing at a tall window and looking down at a market square

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt wanted to unite humanity as one family without princes, nations or churches.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Weishaupt at a window, looking down on the town, the founder's vision of the world.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the founder as the person behind the plan.
storyboard.addedInformation: His ambition was global, not local.

image.subject: a crowded 18th-century Bavarian town square at midday, a Catholic church spire and a royal palace rising behind the rooftops

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt was a radical Enlightenment thinker living in a conservative Catholic state.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The church spire and palace over the square, the conservative power he lived under.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the danger in the founder's situation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Bavaria was dominated by church and crown.

storyboard.claim: To spread a dangerous idea you need a plan for surviving the spread.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A bare question card on the screen with no picture, so the question stands alone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the problem of spreading a dangerous idea.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the next beats as an engineering question.

image.subject: a sealed letter pushed under the heavy wooden door of a stone house on a dark 18th-century street at night

storyboard.claim: Ideas aimed at overthrowing the monarchy and church must travel in secret.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A letter slipped under a door at night, showing covert transmission.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with the method: secret delivery.
storyboard.addedInformation: Covert letters were the medium of the danger.

image.subject: an empty 18th-century European town square at dusk, wet cobblestones, a locked city gate and a single lantern, no people

storyboard.claim: You cannot shout a dangerous idea in a public square; the state would silence you.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty square at dusk, with no people, showing the public place that is closed to such ideas.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the open route is impossible.
storyboard.addedInformation: The square is the place power watches.

image.subject: a folded letter with a red wax seal on a worn wooden table beside a lit candle, a small cipher key lying next to it

storyboard.claim: The idea must move through an encrypted, decentralised network to survive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A wax-sealed letter and cipher key, the tools of a hidden network.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the method that the square-and-state problem demanded.
storyboard.addedInformation: Secrecy was built with letters and codes.

storyboard.claim: The network began very small.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A bare question card, no picture, to let the pause land.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the encrypted network with a question about its size.
storyboard.addedInformation: Prompts the viewer to expect a small number.

storyboard.claim: By December 1779 the Illuminati had only 60 members, confined to a few Bavarian university towns.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large numeral 60 with the date, no picture needed for a number.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the small-start question with the figure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The date and the university-town base.

image.subject: a hand-drawn 18th-century map of southern German lands with fine ink lines linking a few university towns

storyboard.claim: A tiny clique in a few Bavarian towns became a global bogeyman.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A hand-drawn map with ink lines linking the towns, showing the small base.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the number to the geography of the network.
storyboard.addedInformation: The map shows where the network sat.

image.subject: a stone bridge over a river at dusk with a single courier on horseback crossing toward the far bank

storyboard.claim: Weak ties and network contagion made the Illuminati's growth explode.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A courier crossing a bridge, the link between two separate places.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the mechanism behind the map's connections.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the bridge metaphor used later.

storyboard.claim: By the early 1780s the Illuminati had roughly 1300 members.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large numeral 1300 with the date, a plain figure card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the growth the contagion produced.
storyboard.addedInformation: The jump from 60 to about 1300.

image.subject: an 18th-century palace salon at night, gilded mirrors and candles, gentlemen in dark frock coats talking in pairs

storyboard.claim: The members were now infiltrating the ranks of the elite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A palace salon of men in frock coats, the elite spaces the network entered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the growth with the social level it reached.
storyboard.addedInformation: Students became courtiers and officials.

image.subject: the host Niall Ferguson, a British historian in his fifties, short greying hair, dark sport jacket over an open-collar shirt, seated at a wooden desk with books

storyboard.claim: Weak ties matter for understanding how everyday life works.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host at his desk, speaking directly to the viewer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host steps in to slow down and explain.
storyboard.addedInformation: Addresses the viewer personally.

storyboard.claim: Your closest friends share your news, people and places, so you live in a bubble.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three items listed as text, the shared traits of a close circle.
storyboard.onScreenText: SAME NEWS / SAME FRIENDS / SAME PLACES
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the everyday example of the bubble.
storyboard.addedInformation: Three traits that keep a close circle closed.

image.subject: an 18th-century coffee-house counter in a Bavarian town, a waiter and a customer exchanging a few words over a cup

storyboard.claim: A weak tie is an acquaintance you see only now and then, who connects you to a new circle.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A brief exchange across a coffee-house counter, a casual link between strangers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the bubble a bridge: the casual acquaintance.
storyboard.addedInformation: The weak tie is casual, not a close friend.

left.label: CLOSE CIRCLE
left.subject: a tight group of four friends around a candle-lit table in an 18th-century room

right.label: WEAK TIE
right.subject: two acquaintances meeting briefly on a cobbled street corner

storyboard.claim: A weak tie links you to a different cluster of people, while close friends keep you inside.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two side-by-side pictures: a closed group against a brief street meeting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the barista example into a clear contrast.
storyboard.addedInformation: Close friends stay in one cluster; weak ties reach others.

image.subject: a late-18th-century Bavarian university professor in his late twenties, slim, powdered-hair style, dark frock coat with a white cravat, seated at a desk with two open letters side by side

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt used weak ties to jump between social clusters rather than recruiting only friends.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Weishaupt at his desk with two letters, one for each cluster he reached.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the weak-tie idea to the founder.
storyboard.addedInformation: Two letters show two separate circles being connected.

storyboard.claim: The sociologist Mark Granovetter wrote a famous paper on weak ties in the 1970s.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A document card titled The Strength of Weak Ties, no picture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the source of the idea.
storyboard.addedInformation: The 1970s sociologist and his paper title.

image.subject: a stone bridge joining two town districts at dusk, a crowd crossing in both directions over the water

storyboard.claim: Ideas spread across the bridges between communities, not inside tight families.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A bridge with people crossing both ways, the flow between communities.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the bridge image to the general principle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ideas travel between groups, not within them.

image.subject: an 18th-century courier in a dark travelling cloak standing at the doorway of a lodge, a sealed letter in hand

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt used weak ties to move from the students into the broader Freemason networks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A courier at a lodge doorway, the link between the students and the older order.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the next jump in the network, from students to Freemasons.
storyboard.addedInformation: The courier carries the connection.

image.subject: a candle-lit lodge room, a wooden table with a square and compass and an open rulebook, two chairs drawn up

storyboard.claim: The students were brought into the established Freemason lodges.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lodge table with a square and compass and rulebook.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the destination of the courier's connection.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lodge's tools and rulebook.

storyboard.claim: Through the enlightenment salons they recruited a literary giant and the Duke of Saxe-Weimar.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Plain statement card; the names are spoken, and no portrait is authored for these figures.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the lodge network into the salons.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the Weimar court as a recruit.

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt understood viral networks centuries before the internet existed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A timeline card with the 18th century on one end and the internet on the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the network point across time.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the idea in a long historical line.

image.subject: an 18th-century library with tall shelves of ledgers and books, a single candle on a long table, a folded map unrolled across it

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt sounds like an evil genius architect of society.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A library table with a map and candle, the planning room of a mastermind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the image of the mastermind the narration seems to describe.
storyboard.addedInformation: The map and ledgers suggest planning.

storyboard.claim: His private letters show the reality is funnier and less sinister.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A bare question card, no picture, to set up the reveal.
storyboard.onScreenText: BUT WHAT DO THE LETTERS SAY?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the mastermind image toward the letters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Points to the private letters as evidence.

image.subject: a wooden desk with an empty brass cipher wheel, a half-written letter and an unlit candle, no one at the desk

storyboard.claim: The encrypted machine was a bluff; the machine did not exist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty cipher wheel and unfinished letter, the machine is only a prop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the machine question with the bluff.
storyboard.addedInformation: The cipher machine was never built.

storyboard.claim: He designed the idea of a machine, not the machine.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Punchline card with no picture, the reveal lands in text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the bluff with the reversal.
storyboard.addedInformation: Only the idea existed.

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt told a new recruit the ancient order only existed in his mind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A quotation card reading that the order only existed in his mind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the confession that backs the bluff.
storyboard.addedInformation: The founder's own words, to a recruit.

image.subject: a late-18th-century Bavarian university professor in his late twenties, slim, powdered-hair style, dark frock coat with a white cravat, sitting alone at an empty desk in a dim study with one candle

storyboard.claim: There was no ancient architecture of the order; he faked it until it became real.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Weishaupt alone at an empty desk, the order existed only in his head.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the confession with the image of the lonely founder.
storyboard.addedInformation: No ancient structure stood behind the order.

image.subject: two gentlemen in an 18th-century salon examining a folded document as if it were a treasure, candles lit on the wall behind them

storyboard.claim: He sold bored intellectuals the story of a massive ancient conspiracy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two men absorbed in a document, the intellectuals taking the story in.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the audience that bought the story.
storyboard.addedInformation: The recruits were bored intellectuals.

storyboard.claim: The belief in the story is what built the network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Plain statement card, a beat of banter with no picture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A reaction beat that closes the bluff.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the belief back to the building of the network.

image.subject: a single candle burning in a dark lodge room, its light falling on an empty chair and a closed book

storyboard.claim: The order was made real through confidence alone.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lone candle in a dark lodge, belief as the only light.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarises the bluff in one image.
storyboard.addedInformation: Confidence as the source of the network's power.

image.subject: a stone royal palace tower looming over a crowded cobbled town square at dusk, a narrow dark passage running beneath the square

storyboard.claim: The bluff worked as a hidden square running beneath the monarchical tower.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A tower above, a hidden passage below the square, the square-and-tower image of the book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the book's central metaphor for the bluff.
storyboard.addedInformation: Power above, network below.

image.subject: a courier in a dark cloak slipping a folded letter to a man in a doorway on a cobbled street at dusk, two uniformed police officers walking past without looking

storyboard.claim: The network bypassed government sensors and the state police while moving ideas fast.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A letter passed in plain sight while officers walk on, the network slipping past the state.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the tower's blindness to the hidden square.
storyboard.addedInformation: The state police are present and unaware.

image.subject: a crowded 18th-century German tavern at night, men leaning over tables talking over tankards of beer

storyboard.claim: To change society the network had to move from pub talk to real power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A tavern full of men talking, the stage where ideas start.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the hidden network to the question of using it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The tavern as the starting point of ideas.

image.subject: a candle-lit lodge room at night, a map spread across the table and a knot of men in dark coats leaning over it

storyboard.claim: The network had to undergo a fundamental paradoxical mutation to wield power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Men gathered over a map, the group that is about to change shape.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the turn the narration promises.
storyboard.addedInformation: The group must change shape to act.

image.subject: the host Niall Ferguson, a British historian in his fifties, short greying hair, dark sport jacket over an open-collar shirt, seated at a wooden desk with books

storyboard.claim: Networks show how they behave when they meet existing power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host at his desk, returning to the lesson for the viewer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the chunk by returning to the host to frame the lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lesson is about how networks meet existing power.

image.subject: Adolph Knigge, a German baron in his thirties, well-fed, embroidered dark-green court coat, powdered hair, a lace jabot, seated at a candle-lit wooden desk in a 1782 study

storyboard.claim: Knigge, code name Philo, is the man who plans the order in 1782.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Knigge at his desk with a quill and the plan on parchment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the next actor after the flat network of Weishaupt.
storyboard.addedInformation: Knigge's code name is Philo.

image.subject: Adolph Knigge, a German baron in his thirties, well-fed, embroidered dark-green court coat, powdered hair, a lace jabot, bent over a parchment and scratching with a quill

storyboard.claim: Knigge is drafting a new plan for the order by hand.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Knigge writing furiously, quill on parchment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same man as beat 120, now at work on the document.
storyboard.addedInformation: The plan rewrites the order's structure.

image.subject: a close view of a handwritten parchment page on a wooden desk, its lines struck through with heavy quill strokes beside a guttering candle

storyboard.claim: Knigge deliberately crosses out Weishaupt's egalitarian ideals.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Struck-through lines on a manuscript page.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the destruction described in the prior beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The deletion is literal, on the page.

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt wanted a network of absolute equals with no ranks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the egalitarian ideal being destroyed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Weishaupt's ideal was utopian.

storyboard.claim: Knigge judged a flat structure a recipe for irrelevance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the ideal to Knigge's verdict on it.
storyboard.addedInformation: A flat network would not matter to anyone.

storyboard.claim: Knigge wrote highly stratified, fake ranks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the verdict to the solution.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ranks were invented, not inherited.

image.subject: a candle-lit 18th-century lodge room with a long wooden table, a row of sealed certificates and a map, and no people in view

storyboard.claim: Knigge builds a rigid hierarchy out of thin air over the network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty lodge room where the invented structure sits.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains how the hierarchy is laid over the network.
storyboard.addedInformation: A new member no longer joins as a brother.

storyboard.claim: Members advance through four invented ranks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Four ranks listed in order.
storyboard.onScreenText: MANURVAL, MINOR ILLUMINATUS, SCOTTISH KNIGHT, MAGUS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The rigid hierarchy shown as steps.
storyboard.addedInformation: Each rank is earned by proving yourself.

storyboard.claim: A pure flat network is mostly useless for wielding real power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalises the Knigge case into a rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Power needs more than shared ideas.

image.subject: a crowd of ordinary people in plain clothes gathered loosely in a cobbled town square at dusk, seen from behind, with no clear leader

storyboard.claim: Flat networks can share ideas and stage protests but cannot coordinate action.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Loose crowd in a square with no focal leader.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the strengths and limits of a flat network.
storyboard.addedInformation: A crowd without structure is good only for protest.

image.subject: an ordinary man of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind, standing among gold-braided officials in a formal 18th-century hall

storyboard.claim: To conquer a hierarchy, a network must adopt its geometry.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Plain man among formal officials, showing disguise.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from flat failure to the strategy of disguise.
storyboard.addedInformation: The network copies its enemy's structure.

image.subject: a candle-lit 18th-century lodge room with a wooden table, books, a map and a row of chairs arranged for a formal meeting

storyboard.claim: The broader Freemason network was hijacked to build the Illuminati ranks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The lodge room, the hijacked network's setting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns to the Freemason network the Illuminati used.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lodge is the host network for the Illuminati.

storyboard.claim: Nineteenth-century lithographs show Washington proudly wearing his Masonic apron.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the Freemason appeal to elite men.
storyboard.addedInformation: Washington was a Freemason.

storyboard.claim: Washington rejected the British monarchy and walked away from being a king.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the Washington point into irony.
storyboard.addedInformation: He refused to become king in America.

storyboard.claim: Why did a horizontal fraternal network lure powerful men?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the question the next beats answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question names Washington and the Duke of Saxe-Gotha.

image.subject: a German duke in an embroidered court coat seated at a candle-lit lodge table among plain-clothed men, a ribbon catching the light

storyboard.claim: A duke joined the lodge for its secret status.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ducal figure in court coat at a lodge table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with a concrete figure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The duke is powerful and elite.

storyboard.claim: The network offered exclusive hierarchical status.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the reason the powerful joined.
storyboard.addedInformation: The status was exclusive to members.

storyboard.claim: The lodge gave men a new ladder above the uninitiated masses.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three listed phrases.
storyboard.onScreenText: NEW LADDER, SECRET STATUS, ABOVE THE MASSES
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands the status reason into three parts.
storyboard.addedInformation: Men at the top of society wanted an extra tower.

image.subject: a well-dressed gentleman of mid-thirties seen from behind, standing in a candle-lit lodge room in front of a circle of plain-clothed men

storyboard.claim: Men at the top of society joined to feel they were at the top of a secret tower.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A gentleman in a lodge circle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the men described in the prior beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The network elevates its members.

image.subject: Adolph Knigge, a German baron in his thirties, well-fed, embroidered dark-green court coat, powdered hair, a lace jabot, standing apart from a plain-clothed shoemaker across a candle-lit table

storyboard.claim: Knigge understood that a duke would not sit as an equal with a shoemaker.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Baron and shoemaker kept apart at the table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to Knigge with the ego point.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shoemaker is the everyday member.

storyboard.claim: Did Knigge ruin a beautiful flat network?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A speaker challenges Knigge.
storyboard.addedInformation: The network was built on reason and equality.

storyboard.claim: Knigge cynically turned the flat network into an elite tower.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the objection in full.
storyboard.addedInformation: Weishaupt's vision of no ranks was corrupted.

storyboard.claim: Without the fake hierarchy the aristocrats would never have joined.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the objection with history.
storyboard.addedInformation: The fake ranks drew the aristocratic members.

storyboard.claim: Would a flat network of radical students have died out?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pushes the debate forward.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flat network was made of students.

image.subject: a group of young men in plain 1780s clothes drinking beer and arguing around a wooden table in a Bavarian tavern, mugs and a candle on the table

storyboard.claim: A flat student club would have drunk beer, complained and vanished.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Students in a tavern with beer and argument.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the concrete picture behind the claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Complaints about the church would not sustain the group.

storyboard.claim: The structure turned a drinking club into a weapon.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the structure argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Fake ranks, mysteries and initiations did the work.

image.subject: a late-18th-century Bavarian university professor in his late twenties, slim, powdered-hair style, dark frock coat with a white cravat, walking into a formal palace hall to meet state officials

storyboard.claim: The Illuminati could interface directly with state power structures.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Weishaupt entering a palace hall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the hierarchy disguise working on the state.
storyboard.addedInformation: Weishaupt was the professor who founded the lodge.

storyboard.claim: To destroy the tower, the square has to disguise itself as a tower.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quote text only.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE SQUARE DISGUISED AS A TOWER
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sums up the paradox just described.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the central paradox of the chapter.

storyboard.claim: The shadow hierarchy gained the attention of the real one and let the Illuminati punch above their weight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the paradox worked.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shadow tower gained real attention.

image.subject: a Bavarian official's letter with a red wax seal lying on a wooden desk beside an open ledger, a candle burning down

storyboard.claim: Bavarian authorities found out, panicked and outlawed the Illuminati in 1784.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Official letter with seal on a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Ends the Illuminati stretch with the state's response.
storyboard.addedInformation: The authorities acted by decree.

storyboard.claim: The square must interface with the tower to achieve true power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalises the pattern and leads to the next case.
storyboard.addedInformation: The most successful network in modern history comes next.

image.subject: a gilded 19th-century hall in Vienna where emperors, kings and diplomats in gold braid and medals stand around a large table after the Napoleonic wars

storyboard.claim: The Congress of Vienna in 1815 ended the Napoleonic Wars.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gilded hall with diplomats around a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the next case study.
storyboard.addedInformation: The wars had lasted decades.

image.subject: an opulent 19th-century room of emperors and kings covered in gold braid and medals, gathered around a giant sweeping map of Europe

storyboard.claim: The room of Vienna is opulent and filled with gold and braid.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Crowded gilded room with the map in view.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the scene described in beat 151.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emperors, kings and diplomats are all present.

image.subject: a diplomat in a gold-braided coat leaning over a large map of Europe, drawing a line across it with a pen

storyboard.claim: Diplomats casually redraw borders and trade millions of lives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A diplomat drawing a border line.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the action in the room.
storyboard.addedInformation: The redrawing traded lives.

storyboard.claim: The Congress was called the cake of kings, the top-down power of monarchy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quote text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the room's power.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phrase is the historians' own label.

storyboard.claim: Simultaneously, a different kind of power operates just outside the room.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Place text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the official room to the counting house.
storyboard.addedInformation: The different power is horizontal.

image.subject: Mayer Amschel Rothschild, an 18th-century Frankfurt merchant-banker in his fifties, stout, dark wool coat, round spectacles, ledger in hand, standing in the doorway of a busy counting house

storyboard.claim: A frantic Rothschild counting house operates just outside the official room.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rothschild in a counting house doorway with a ledger.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the Rothschild network.
storyboard.addedInformation: The counting house is busy and frantic.

image.subject: an ordinary courier in a mud-spattered riding coat hurrying out of a doorway, a leather pouch of sealed letters under his arm

storyboard.claim: Couriers move information and money faster than any king's army can march.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Courier with a letter pouch hurrying from a door.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the couriers the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Money moves faster than armies.

storyboard.claim: The Rothschilds ran a decentralised family network with brothers in several cities.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the family members in the network.
storyboard.addedInformation: Nathan in London, James in Paris, Solomon in Vienna, Carl in Naples, Amsel in Frankfurt.

image.subject: a long wooden counting-house table with five sealed letters laid out in a row, each addressed to a different European capital, a brass scale beside them

storyboard.claim: Five brothers in five cities form five nodes constantly communicating.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Five letters in a row on a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the family names into a visible network.
storyboard.addedInformation: The letters show constant communication.

image.subject: Niall Ferguson, a British historian in his fifties, short greying hair, dark sport jacket over an open-collar shirt, seated at a wooden desk with books and a stack of old ledgers beside him

storyboard.claim: Information and money move across borders, so power today is shaped by that movement.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host at his desk with books and ledgers, the subject of the next idea.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the Rothschild courier thread and turns it toward today.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the chapter as a question about modern power.

image.subject: a gilded quill pen resting on a printed 1815 map of Europe in a candle-lit palace study, a line of fresh ink drawn across the map

storyboard.claim: Kings draw borders on maps with their pens.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A quill drawing a border across a printed map of Europe.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the contrast between kings and networks.
storyboard.addedInformation: The kings hold the pen that draws borders.

image.subject: a leather purse spilling gold coins across an open ledger in a Frankfurt counting house with tall shelves behind it, dim winter light from a window

storyboard.claim: Financial networks control whether borders survive, not the kings.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A purse of gold coins on a ledger in a counting house.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the pen image: the pen draws, the purse decides.
storyboard.addedInformation: Money decides whether the borders hold.

storyboard.claim: States must pay for armies, peace and infrastructure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three cost items listed in plain type.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what the kings had to pay for.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the three big state costs.

storyboard.claim: Taxes arrive once a year but armies are paid every day.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A large two-part number contrast in text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the gap that forces states to borrow.
storyboard.addedInformation: The timing mismatch is the core problem.

image.subject: a row of sovereign bond certificates stacked on a banker's desk, each printed with a royal crest, in a Frankfurt counting house

storyboard.claim: The Rothschild network came to dominate the sovereign bond market.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stacked royal bond certificates on a banker's desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cash gap leads to borrowing through bonds.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the bond market the network controlled.

image.subject: a Victorian London newspaper kiosk at dusk, broadsheets stacked under a gas lamp, a few pedestrians in dark wool coats passing by

storyboard.claim: Jump forward to 1894 London.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A Victorian newspaper kiosk under a gas lamp at dusk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves the story from the bond market to the press of the 1890s.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the date and city for the cartoon that follows.

image.subject: a stack of 1890s London broadsheet newspapers folded open to a page of printed political cartoons, black ink on yellowed paper

storyboard.claim: A famous 1894 anti-Rothschild political cartoon circulated in the press.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Yellowed broadsheet pages with printed cartoon panels.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Points to the cartoon the host is about to describe.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cartoon was printed press material.

image.subject: a heavy brass-bound chest of gold coins, its lid open, in a dim 19th-century counting house with a shuttered window

storyboard.claim: The cartoon depicts a menacing force feeding on gold.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An open chest of gold coins in dim light.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the cartoon's gold imagery in place of the creature itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the gold that the cartoon's creature was feeding on.

image.subject: an antique terrestrial globe on a wooden stand in a London library, lit by a single lamp, its painted continents worn at the edges

storyboard.claim: The network seemed to reach every continent.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worn antique globe lit by one lamp.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the cartoon's reach to a real object.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the global reach visible.

left.label: THE TOWER
left.subject: a stone royal palace at dusk with lit windows and guards standing at a closed iron gate

right.label: THE SQUARE
right.subject: a crowded 19th-century European town square at dusk, revolutionary banners hanging above cobblestones

storyboard.claim: A decentralized network looked terrifying to vertical towers of power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two pictures side by side: a closed royal palace gate and a crowded square.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the tower-square contrast the cartoon embodies.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the viewer both sides of the power contrast.

storyboard.claim: The Rothschilds had no army, king or country yet touched everything.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A rhetorical question in text.
storyboard.onScreenText: NO ARMY / NO KING / NO COUNTRY
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the towers feared the network.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists what the Rothschilds lacked.

storyboard.claim: Refusing to buy a nation's debt could ruin its economy, making the network subversive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A bold closing line in text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question just asked.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the lever the network held over states.

image.subject: an ordinary person of mid-thirties in plain clothes, seen from behind, standing in a crowded town square at dusk and looking up at a tall stone tower

storyboard.claim: The square appears to dominate the tower.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure from behind facing a stone tower across a dusk square.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the claim into an image of the square facing the tower.
storyboard.addedInformation: The everyman stands for the square.

image.subject: a historian's hands turning the pages of an open 19th-century archive ledger with handwritten columns of figures in a quiet library

storyboard.claim: The popular myth differs from the documented record.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Hands turning pages of an archive ledger.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the myth to the evidence.
storyboard.addedInformation: The record is a ledger, not a rebellion.

image.subject: a row of gilded palace windows lit at dusk on a grand imperial street in Vienna, a carriage waiting at the entrance

storyboard.claim: The Rothschilds financed empires, not revolutions.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A grand imperial palace at dusk with a waiting carriage.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the empire the record says they supported.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the financing in an imperial capital.

storyboard.claim: If they could break the king, why not do it?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A direct question in text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the puzzle the next beat answers.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the paradox.

image.subject: an old royal bond with a faded crown seal, tied with a ribbon, lying on a counting-house desk beside a sealed letter of demand

storyboard.claim: New governments would default on old royal debts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A faded royal bond tied with ribbon on a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers why the network needed the kings.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the debts that would go unpaid.

image.subject: an 18th-century Frankfurt merchant-banker in his fifties, stout, dark wool coat, round spectacles, ledger in hand, standing in a counting house

storyboard.claim: The Rothschilds became stabilizers of the monarchy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The banker with ledger, standing in a counting house.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers who would pay the bonds.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the named banker on screen as the stabilizer.

image.subject: a royal palace at dusk with lit windows, seen across a river, the palace's stone walls reflected in still water

storyboard.claim: The network's survival depended on the survival of the state towers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lit royal palace reflected in still water.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the state tower the network depended on.
storyboard.addedInformation: The palace is the state whose survival matters.

image.subject: a courier in a dark travelling coat arriving at a Frankfurt bank doorway with a leather satchel of letters, a stagecoach waiting in the street

storyboard.claim: Kings had to stay on thrones so interest kept arriving in Frankfurt and London.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A courier with a satchel at a bank door beside a waiting stagecoach.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the reasoning in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the courier carrying interest payments.

image.subject: a counting-house window overlooking a crowded town square at dusk, ledgers stacked on the sill and revolutionary banners hanging across the street

storyboard.claim: The square ended up financing the tower and became the status quo.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A counting-house window looking onto a dusk square.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pulls the square and the tower into one view.
storyboard.addedInformation: The counting house sits between the square and the state.

storyboard.claim: The kings kept their crowns and the network got rich.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two outcomes listed in plain type.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarises the bargain.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the two sides of the deal.

image.subject: a long wooden table in a candle-lit lodge room, an old map of Europe spread across it with thin red and blue threads pinned between cities

storyboard.claim: Hidden networks govern visible structures.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A map of Europe with red and blue threads pinned between cities.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the banking story to the general claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: The threads show the hidden web.

storyboard.claim: Leave the royal courts for a mundane setting.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A place label in text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from Europe's courts to the reformatory.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the next location.

image.subject: a dusty classroom chalkboard in a 1930s girls' reformatory school in Hudson, New York, wooden desks empty in the late afternoon light

storyboard.claim: The setting is a chalkboard at a New York girls' reformatory in 1932.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A dusty chalkboard in an empty 1930s classroom.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves to the new setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets place and year.

image.subject: a 1930s American psychiatrist in his forties, dark three-piece suit with the tie loosened, chalk in hand, standing beside a dusty classroom chalkboard

storyboard.claim: Jacob Moreno invented the sociological study of networks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A psychiatrist in a 1930s suit with chalk beside a chalkboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the person from the setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the psychiatrist who founded network sociology.

image.subject: a dusty chalkboard covered in tangled, chaotic webs of chalk lines linking rows of circles

storyboard.claim: Moreno drew tangled webs of circles and lines called sociograms.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A chalkboard with a tangled web of circles and lines.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the drawing the psychiatrist just made.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the form of a sociogram.

image.subject: a group of young women in plain 1930s dresses seated on a wooden bench in a reformatory courtyard, seen from behind

storyboard.claim: Sociograms mapped the hidden social dynamics of the girls in the reformatory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young women on a bench in a courtyard, seen from behind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the people the chalk diagram maps.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the mapped group on screen.

left.label: HATE
left.subject: two chalk circles joined by a short hard red line on a dusty blackboard

right.label: FRIENDSHIP
right.subject: two chalk circles joined by a short soft blue line on a dusty blackboard

storyboard.claim: Red lines show hate and rejection, blue lines show friendship and attraction.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two chalk pairs of circles, one joined by red, one by blue.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the colour code of the sociogram.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines the two line types.

image.subject: an iron-railed gate of a 1930s reformatory standing open onto a dirt road at dusk, empty footprints in the dust

storyboard.claim: The school faced an epidemic of girls running away.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An open reformatory gate onto a dusty road at dusk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the crisis that the chalk diagram addresses.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the exit the runaways took.

storyboard.claim: The administration looked only at the official structure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three things the administration examined, listed in plain type.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE LAYOUT / THE RULES / THE RECORDS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the administration was clueless.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the three official things they checked.

image.subject: a 1930s office bulletin board with a pinned organisation chart of boxes and lines carrying typed names

storyboard.claim: The administration was looking at the org chart.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A pinned organisation chart on an office board.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the official structure just listed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the chart being looked at.

image.subject: a shelf of printed official rulebooks beside a single open notebook with pencil lines drawn across its pages

storyboard.claim: The official rules did not matter; the invisible network did.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rulebooks on a shelf and an open notebook with pencil lines.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the official structure to the invisible one.
storyboard.addedInformation: The notebook is the network being traced.

image.subject: a young woman in a plain 1930s dress answering questions across a wooden table while a psychiatrist in a dark suit writes notes

storyboard.claim: By asking the girls who they liked and hated, the hidden web emerged.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An interview across a table, the writer taking notes.
storyboard.onScreenText: WHO THEY LIKED / WHO THEY HATED
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the method behind the diagram.
storyboard.addedInformation: The method was asking the girls directly.

image.subject: a hand-drawn network map spread across a wooden desk, a few dark hub circles larger than the rest and one lonely circle set apart

storyboard.claim: The map reveals hubs of influence, isolated girls and rumour channels.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A hand-drawn network map with hubs and one isolated circle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes what the map shows.
storyboard.addedInformation: Adds the isolated node and rumour channels.

image.subject: an ordinary person in plain clothes, mid-thirties, seen from behind, standing in a modern open-plan office with small groups of coworkers talking

storyboard.claim: Your success is governed by invisible networks at your workplace.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure from behind in an office with small groups talking.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the reformatory lesson to the listener.
storyboard.addedInformation: Brings the idea to the viewer's own office.

storyboard.claim: Influence is not about the official org chart or title.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A bold closing line in text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the workplace application.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dismisses the title as the measure of influence.

storyboard.claim: Who do people go to for help or the real story? Almost never the person at the top.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A question in text.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE REAL STORY / NOT THE TOP
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks who the real hub is.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the answer about centrality.

image.subject: a chalk diagram of seven small circles where one circle in the middle connects a line to every other circle

storyboard.claim: Your position depends on betweenness centrality in the hidden network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Seven circles with one central node connected to all.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the measure the previous question pointed to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the central node as the betweenness hub.

image.subject: Niall Ferguson, a British historian in his fifties, short greying hair, dark sport jacket over an open-collar shirt, seated at a wooden desk with books, sketching a small cluster of dots joined by lines on a notepad

storyboard.claim: Betweenness centrality is a foundational network measure of how much information must pass through a given node.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host at his desk sketching a network of dots and lines.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the new concept after the tower-and-square framing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines betweenness as the share of paths that run through a node.

image.subject: an ordinary person of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind, standing in a doorway between a quiet engineering room of desks and a noisy bright marketing office

storyboard.claim: A person with no high title can hold power by linking two clusters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure from behind in the doorway joining two separate office groups.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the abstract measure a human position.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the two clusters: introverted engineers and extroverted marketers.

image.subject: a candle-lit 18th-century lodge room with a wooden table, books and a map, a small group of men in dark coats standing in a half-circle around it

storyboard.claim: The connector holds immense informal power that is invisible on the org chart.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lodge table where a half-circle of men gathers around a shared map.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Links the connector to the invisible square.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the connector role to the square outside the tower's formal hierarchy.

image.subject: a long office floor of desks seen from a glass walkway, workers seated in small clusters with one figure walking between them

storyboard.claim: The invisible square decides how the tower works day to day.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A long office floor with clusters of workers and one connecting walker.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the concept to everyday workplace effect.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the informal network operating inside a formal building.

storyboard.claim: The math of this network traces back to a puzzle in 1735.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large year number 1735 on a plain field.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from daily life to the historical origin of the math.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dates the origin of the network puzzle.

storyboard.claim: The city of Konigsberg in Prussia was built around the Pregel River.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Place card naming Konigsberg, Prussia.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the setting of the bridge puzzle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Locates the river city and its two islands.

storyboard.claim: Two islands were linked to each other and the mainland by exactly seven bridges.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three short list items naming the islands, bridges and walk.
storyboard.onScreenText: TWO ISLANDS / SEVEN BRIDGES / ONE WALK
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the city's physical layout.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the exact bridge count of seven.

storyboard.claim: Could a walk cross all seven bridges exactly once?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question card asking if all seven can be crossed once.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the layout into the puzzle.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the exact question locals struggled with for years.

image.subject: an 18th-century ink map of the river city with two islands and seven bridges, spread on a candle-lit library table, no lettering

storyboard.claim: People walked in circles trying to solve the bridge problem for years.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ink map of the river city with islands and seven bridges on a library table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the physical puzzle the question refers to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualises the river, islands and bridges of Konigsberg.

image.subject: a candle-lit library table with a stack of mathematics books, an open notebook covered in dots and lines, and a quill

storyboard.claim: Euler proved the walk impossible by inventing a new branch of mathematics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mathematics books and a notebook of dots and lines on a library table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the mathematician who answered the puzzle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names Euler and his new branch of mathematics.

image.subject: a candle-lit library table with a folded city map pushed aside, an inkwell and a bare sheet of paper

storyboard.claim: Euler ignored the physical map, the island sizes and the bridge materials.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A folded map pushed aside on a bare table with a blank sheet.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains how Euler's method differed.
storyboard.addedInformation: States that size and material of the bridges did not matter.

storyboard.claim: Euler reduced the city to nodes, the land masses, and edges, the bridges.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows from stripping away physical detail.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines the two abstract parts of a network.

left.label: LAND MASSES
left.subject: a pen-and-ink map of two river islands joined to the banks by seven bridges on a library table

right.label: NODES AND EDGES
right.subject: the same islands reduced to a few dots joined by plain lines on a blank sheet of paper

storyboard.claim: The city becomes a graph of nodes and edges.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Left, the islands and bridges as drawn land; right, the same as dots and lines.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the abstraction from the previous line.
storyboard.addedInformation: Pairs the physical city with its graph reduction.

image.subject: a sheet of graph paper on a wooden table with a few dots joined by lines, one dot circled in ink, beside a candle

storyboard.claim: A walk needs a graph with exactly two nodes of odd degree or none.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Graph paper with dots and lines, one dot circled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the abstraction to the proof's condition.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the odd-degree condition for a continuous walk.

storyboard.claim: Entering and leaving a node needs an even number of edges unless it is the start or end.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only, conversational.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A conversational clarification of the proof.
storyboard.addedInformation: Explains why even edge counts matter at each node.

storyboard.claim: Konigsberg had four land masses, each with an odd number of bridges, so the walk was impossible.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three list items summarising the verdict.
storyboard.onScreenText: FOUR LAND MASSES / ODD BRIDGES / NO WALK
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the proof to Konigsberg.
storyboard.addedInformation: Confirms all four land masses have odd bridge counts.

image.subject: an ordinary person of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind at a window, looking down on a crowded 18th-century street of pedestrians and carriages

storyboard.claim: If human behaviour reduces to nodes and edges, it might be fully controllable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Figure from behind at a window over a busy street.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the math to the question of human behaviour.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the naive assumption that networks can be engineered.

storyboard.claim: Does the map of human links mean behaviour is totally controllable?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question card on the assumption.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Poses the question the next beats answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the contradiction with predictability.

image.subject: Mark Zuckerberg, a 21st-century American tech founder in his thirties, short brown hair, plain grey T-shirt under a dark hoodie, no tie, standing before a row of server racks in a cool data centre

storyboard.claim: Modern mappers like Facebook map friendships and believe they can control the network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Zuckerberg before server racks in a data centre.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the mapping idea into the modern era.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names Facebook as a modern mapper of social links.

image.subject: a wooden desk with a ledger, a closed book and a map pinned to a plaster wall, a single candle burning

storyboard.claim: Engineering the links assumes the network is predictable, which the math contradicts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Desk with ledger, book and map under a candle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the control assumption.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the claim that the network is not predictable.

storyboard.claim: Why are social networks unstable, and why do revolutions happen overnight?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question card asking about instability and overnight revolutions.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the paradox from the contradiction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames instability and sudden revolution as the puzzle.

image.subject: a printed sociogram on paper, dots and lines spread across a wooden table in a candle-lit library, beside a map and a ledger

storyboard.claim: We can map the current structure of nodes, but the network also has emergent properties.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sociogram diagram on paper on a library table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Acknowledges the sociogram before adding dynamics.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces sociograms as a way to draw current structure.

storyboard.claim: A human social network is dynamic and constantly shifting, not a static stone bridge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the difference from a physical bridge.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts a static bridge with a shifting human network.

image.subject: a stone square at dusk with two separate groups of people on either side of a narrow gap, one thin strand of light crossing the gap

storyboard.claim: A single new connection between two clusters can cause a massive phase transition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two groups in a square divided by a gap, one strand of light crossing it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the dynamic claim a visible form.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines the trigger as one link between separate clusters.

image.subject: a candle-lit dining table in an 18th-century room with a dozen guests in small clusters, each deep in a separate low-voiced conversation

storyboard.claim: A quiet dinner party has several disconnected clusters talking separately.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dining table with guests in separate clusters.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the abstract clusters in a familiar scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows multiple disconnected clusters in one room.

image.subject: an ordinary person of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind, leaning into a dinner table to speak loudly across two groups of seated guests

storyboard.claim: A shocking piece of gossip, loud enough for two groups to hear, bridges them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Figure from behind leaning across two seated groups.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the bridging event to the dinner scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the bridging act as one person speaking across groups.

image.subject: a candle-lit dinner room where all the guests have turned toward one table, forming a single close circle

storyboard.claim: Every person stops and joins one highly charged unified conversation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Guests turned into one circle around a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the result of the gossip crossing the gap.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualises the merged group after the bridge forms.

storyboard.claim: The whole room's structure changed in one second from one new piece of information.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large stat: 1 SECOND.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Quantifies the speed of the transition.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the transition took one second.

image.subject: Henry Kissinger, an elderly American statesman in a dark suit, white hair combed back, heavy-framed glasses, seated at a long table in a stone room with papers spread before him

storyboard.claim: The tower believes it perfectly controls its environment, until a rumour crosses a weak tie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Kissinger seated at a long table with papers in a stone room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the room to the tower's view of control.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places a statesman who invoked networks as the tower's voice.

image.subject: a folded letter passed from hand to hand across a crowded 19th-century city square

storyboard.claim: A rumour spreads across a weak tie and the structure collapses.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Folded letter passed hand to hand in a crowded square.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the weak tie a visible carrier.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows a weak tie carrying information across a crowd.

image.subject: a large, peaceful crowd filling a city square at dusk, people with their backs to the camera, no readable banners

storyboard.claim: The Arab Spring is a modern example of a massive phase transition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large peaceful crowd filling a city square at dusk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the phase transition a modern example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the Arab Spring as the modern case.

image.subject: a scholar in a candle-lit library reading a ledger, a stack of books and loose papers beside him on a wooden table

storyboard.claim: Networks cannot be neatly engineered the way hierarchies are engineered.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Scholar reading a ledger in a library.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Draws the conclusion from the examples.
storyboard.addedInformation: States that networks are inherently unpredictable, unlike hierarchies.

image.subject: a tall stone tower with narrow windows seen from the square below, a crowd of people milling beneath it

storyboard.claim: The tower looks down at the square's chaotic web of shifting alliances and panics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stone tower viewed from a crowded square below.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the tower-and-square metaphor.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the institutional fear of the unpredictable square.

image.subject: a candle-lit library table with an open folio, loose papers and a closed ledger beside a dark window

storyboard.claim: The next beat is the myth of the omnipotent network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Open folio and papers on a library table by a dark window.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridges to the next myth beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the myth that the next beat examines.

storyboard.claim: When the tower gets scared, it starts seeing ghosts, so we go to the early 1900s.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only as the time transition.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the myth to the historical case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the early 1900s as the example period.

image.subject: a smoke-filled private club in London, men in deep leather armchairs around a low table with glasses of port, seen from the doorway

storyboard.claim: A posh London club is where the early-1900s planning happens.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Smoke-filled club with leather armchairs and port glasses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves to the historical setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the scene in a London club in the early 1900s.

image.subject: a grey-haired British man in a dark Edwardian suit seated in a leather armchair in a smoke-filled club, a notebook on his knee

storyboard.claim: Lord Alfred Milner's so-called kindergarten, later the round table, meets here.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Edwardian man in a leather armchair with a notebook.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the group in the club.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names Milner and his kindergarten group.

image.subject: an ordinary early-1900s British man in a dark tailored suit, seen from behind, leaning over a notebook in a leather armchair

storyboard.claim: They were young, ambitious, highly educated British imperialists, including writers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Edwardian man from behind taking notes in a leather armchair.
